name: Insurance
blurb: Underwriting, claims triage, and fraud detection under active regulator supervision, with NAIC, AM Best, and the Evident insurance index.

points.desc: The NAIC model bulletin on insurers' use of AI - adopted by a growing majority of states - is the operative US governance document for the sector.
points.name: NAIC set the supervisory frame

points.desc: Outside-in benchmarking of the major global insurers on AI talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency - the sector's comparative maturity scoreboard.
points.name: The Evident AI Index benchmarks insurers

reading.body:
The operative constraint on insurance AI is regulatory: the NAIC model bulletin, adopted by a growing majority of states, sets algorithmic-fairness expectations for underwriting, claims triage, and fraud detection.

The pattern is supervision plus external benchmarking. NAIC appears twice, as the source of the model bulletin and as the body setting model-governance expectations, which makes it the binding layer over underwriting AI. AM Best folds innovation and digital maturity into credit opinion, and the Evident AI Index scores insurers on talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency. Together these measure governance and capability, not model output.

The data does not cover compute, data center capacity, or grid constraints, so it cannot support claims about infrastructure limits on insurance AI. It also gives no adoption counts or performance figures beyond the statement that a growing majority of states have adopted the bulletin. What it establishes is that the sector's AI deployments are named and supervised, with fairness expectations attached to the three core use cases.

summary: Underwriting, claims triage, and fraud detection are the deployments regulators are actively supervising.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks firms whether they used AI in the last two weeks, reports 41.0% for finance and insurance (NAICS 52), up from 36.5% in the prior period. That figure covers the whole finance and insurance sector rather than insurance alone, and the survey first asked the question in September 2023. No insurance-specific adoption rate appears in the material.

The NAIC describes where the technology actually sits in insurance operations: underwriting, pricing, customer service, claims handling, marketing, and fraud detection. Its page gives concrete examples, AI-powered chatbots answering common customer questions and assisting with simple transactions at any time of day, and claims processing that estimates repair costs or assesses damage from photos and historical data. The NAIC also notes AI's ability to analyze unstructured data such as text, images, and video, and the possibility of shifting insurers from a detect and repair approach toward predict and prevent, identifying risks earlier and helping customers avoid losses.

On money and vendors, the harvested material is thin. The Evident AI Index benchmarks AI adoption across financial services and publishes an insurance edition, the 2026 Evident AI Index for Insurance, which ranks leading insurers and profiles where the technology is starting to unlock value and where insurers should focus next. Evident also runs an invitation-only AI Symposium for senior AI leaders in finance. The excerpts name no insurance software vendors and cite no spending figures, so nothing more specific can be said from this material.

On returns, the sources are similarly quiet. Evident frames its index around where AI is starting to unlock value, but the excerpt reports no measured ROI. The NAIC page describes expected benefits in operational terms, faster service and better risk identification, without quantifying them. A reader looking for hard return evidence will not find it here.

The regulatory posture is the best-documented part. The NAIC states that insurers using AI remain responsible for complying with insurance laws, regulations, insurance standards, and consumer protection rules, including fairness, accuracy, and avoiding unfair discrimination, and that state regulators oversee AI use and may require companies to explain how tools are used in underwriting, pricing, marketing, or claims decisions. Human oversight remains an important part of insurance decision-making. The NAIC formed the Innovation Cybersecurity and Technology (H) Committee in 2021, and in 2019 established the Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (H) Working Group, which developed regulatory principles adopted by the full NAIC membership at the 2020 Summer National Meeting. Beginning in 2021 the Working Group surveyed insurers by line of business on AI and machine learning use and governance controls, with aggregate reports on private passenger auto, homeowners, life, and health issued in December 2022, August 2023, December 2023, and May 2025. This site's own sourced points add that the NAIC model bulletin on insurers' use of AI has been adopted by a growing majority of states and is the operative US governance document for the sector, and that AM Best evaluates innovation and digital maturity as part of its assessments, bringing technology capability into credit opinions.

The NAIC also flags a practical risk: large language models do not truly understand context and meaning the way humans do and may generate information that sounds accurate but is incorrect, so AI-generated information should be reviewed carefully, especially for important decisions. It expects AI to support rather than replace actuaries, underwriters, claims professionals, agents, and customer service representatives, who still review information, exercise judgment, and work directly with consumers. For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material points to a sector where adoption is rising, use cases are well established across the value chain, and the binding constraint is governance: state-level supervision, explainability expectations, and human review are treated as conditions of use rather than optional extras.

https://content.naic.org/.brief: The homepage invites users to explore recent publications, the latest news articles, new federal and legislative news, and model laws. It presents these resources as a way to help inform their approach. The page is organized to provide quick access to up-to-date regulatory information. Users can browse the listed materials to stay current with relevant laws and guidance.

https://content.naic.org/insurance-topic.brief: NAIC created the Innovation Cybersecurity and Technology Committee in 2021 to discuss how new technology, including AI, affects insurance regulation. The Big Data and Artificial Intelligence Working Group, established in 2019, produced regulatory principles on AI that NAIC members adopted in 2020, and has been surveying insurers across lines of business, issuing reports in December 2022, August 2023, December 2023, and May 2025. AI is applied in underwriting, pricing, customer service, claims handling, marketing, and fraud detection, and can help insurers shift from a “detect and repair” approach to a “predict and prevent” strategy. The Working Group notes that while AI can automate many tasks, human oversight remains essential for compliance with fairness, accuracy, and consumer protection rules.
